title: The Measurement of Jerusalem and the Young Man
english: Having been assigned the interpretations of the Savior, whom the prophet Jeremiah shows, saying: 'Behold, a man, Rising is his name' (Jer 27:2). And Rising is called 'the true light.' And John the Baptist said concerning him: 'A man comes after me who has become before me' (John 1:15).

This man, being a builder of Jerusalem, architecturally measures its width and length, having previously laid its foundations and having been cast down, and after the destruction which he underwent from the coming of wars and those capturing her, so that he may lay the foundations in the proper places, symmetrically and in order, upon which it was fitting for her walls to be raised.

And there was shown to the prophet a geometric measuring line, woven from various architectural threads, so that the previously prophesied might be fulfilled in: 'And a measure shall be stretched out over Jerusalem yet again' (Zech 2:2). And not far from the Savior being the architect, according to what was said concerning 'the city of the Lord of Powers,' that: 'God has founded it for eternity,' the apostle Paul is writing in concert concerning this divine city, which is expected by all those having pleased through faith, thus: 'For they received the city having foundations, of whom God is the craftsman and builder' (Heb 11:10).

The angels and holy men who rebuild with him, like excellent craftsmen, hold the aforementioned geometric measuring line in his hand called the practical power. Paul indeed writes concerning himself: 'As a wise architect, I laid a foundation' (1 Cor 3:10).

Furthermore, in Ezekiel, a man is seen holding a builder's rod and a reed to measure and found the holy temple of God (Ezek 40:5). In such a way he measured and crafted the building, it is possible to know, the one reading the prophet.

Since therefore the Savior is also shown to be the builder of the upper and spiritual Jerusalem, and even more he shall be shown by the Father pointing him out and saying: 'This one shall build my city,' and those contributing as both angels and men to the rebuilding of the city, according to all the clarifications assigned, ought to follow the man shown by the prophet Zechariah saying: 'Behold, a man, and in his hand a geometric measuring line' (Zech 2:1), and: 'Where is he going?' (Zech 2:2) so that...

By chance, one holding the geometric cord approaches to measure how much the width and length of Jerusalem is. For he is taking care to build well, knowing the location and the opportunity of the plots, so that each of the parts of the city, having been taken with appropriate width and length, may place the divisions, temples, monasteries, streets, and squares in harmony, so that in these streets the wisdom of God may carry itself with boldness, being proclaimed on the edges of the city walls according to what is philosophized in Proverbs, as if to say to those guarding this holy city to proclaim Him within it and upon its walls, day and night, by no means being silent but always speaking things for the salvation of its citizens.

Thrice Jerusalem has been often assigned by analogy, both of the visible soul and of the 'glorious Church not having a pillar or a support' because of holiness and fullness, and of the heavenly city of the living God, in every way to have its width and length measured by him having the geometric cord in his hand, a man being assigned by him having the reason of wisdom and knowledge. And behold, the angel speaking in me stood. And another angel was coming out to meet him, and said to him, saying: 'Run and speak to that young man there, saying.' He says that he saw the angel standing speaking in himself, and another angel coming out saying to him: 'Running, say to this young man what it is time to say.'

In many ways it has been interpreted before what it is that is spoken in the prophet by a divine angel and how this is made manifest, especially when the promise comes from another angel coming out. For it is not possible for the things being announced to be heard while remaining within and by oneself, but by coming out through condescension. Indeed, the showing of the things of the mystery happens not toward a man but toward a young man. For just as the holy man is a young man toward the divine angels, especially when he exists clothed as a young man, as it was said concerning him in the divine Proverbs such as this: 'A young man with the holy one, and his way is straight.' title: Participation in Virtue and the Fruitfulness of the Holy City
english: Is not the way of the one traveling with holiness straight? Regarding those having such a participation in virtue, John in his epistle addresses them, saying: 'I wrote to you, young men, that you are strong and have overcome the evil one.' (1 John 2:14). Everyone alone who thus waters according to the mind is instructed by the one coming forth, the angel, to speak the following things made clear.

And see if it is in the power of the one coming forth, the angel of the same power, to be said by the choir of the saints: 'You went out for the salvation of your people, to save your Christs,' and to him: 'I went forth from God and I have come.' For salvation and divine enrichment become the race of men cast out from paradise, having trodden the divine laws, when the 'angel of the will' of the 'great' God comes forth in order that he might lead in through obedience and divine instruction the one cast out, saying: 'Today with me you shall be in paradise.' The one coming forth promises to show great things concerning the spiritual Jerusalem, which the following word, having such a character, signifies.

Jerusalem shall be inhabited abundantly from a multitude of men and beasts in its midst, and I shall be to her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I shall be in her glory in its midst (Zechariah 2:8-9). In whatever way all the trees in paradise bear much fruit, so also the holy city Jerusalem is inhabited abundantly, having a multitude of men and beasts in its midst; for it is neither fitting nor possible for the divine and holy city to be found unfruitful, the unfruitful tree being cut off and given out to the fire.

Such was the one to whom the holy one cries: 'Therefore God brings you to an end, to uproot you and to transplant you from a dwelling, and your root from the land of the living' (Psalm 52:8), while everyone remaining in the house of God says thankfully: 'I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God' (Psalm 52:8). For how can the one dwelling in the house of God, nourished by the divine light, not bear fruit, in doing what is necessary and thinking the pious doctrines? Thus the man blessed in the first Psalm was a fruitful tree; for it has been said concerning him: 'He shall be like the tree planted by the streams of water, which brings forth its fruit...'

title: The Flight from the North and the Gathering to Zion
english: It consumes, 'a consuming fire,' especially those thorns and briers that bear fruit, and even more so those that are cut off and thrown out because they do not make good fruit but destructive and poisonous fruit. Similarly to the holy city, the Lord is said to be around the people in one of the songs of the ascents: 'The Lord is around his people' (Ps 121:4).

Just as a wall of fire has become around Jerusalem the fallen, and has risen up as a glory in its midst, due to the being glorified by divinity and blessedness of those dwelling in the holy city which is encircled by God, about which the hymn-singer said, rather towards it: 'The city of God was spoken of as having been glorified' (Ps 48:14), and also: 'Great and exceedingly praiseworthy is the Lord, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain' (Ps 87:2).

And it will also be to us by the grace of the beneficent God to bear the fruits of the Spirit, so that around us the Lord might become like a fiery wall, illuminating and guarding us, while consuming the enemies coming to cast us down, so that we might triumphantly declare, showing the incorruptible city: 'Behold, a strong city and our salvation.'

'O, O, flee from the land of the north,' says the Lord (Zech 2:6); 'for from the four winds of heaven I will gather you,' says the Lord; 'be saved, you who dwell in the daughter of Babylon' (Zech 2:6).

The word stirs up those scattered 'in the north, where the evils are burned up from the face of those dwelling in the land,' concisely desiring the flight to take place from the hands [of the enemy], which is signified by the name of the north, doubling the epithet of the exhortation, saying: 'O, O, flee from the land of the north.' He flees from the hands and from the punishment of poets being eager for repentance, going out from evil. The same as fleeing from the land of the north is: 'Turn away from evil,' and: 'Cease from your evils.'

And this is fulfilled when an abstinence from every kind of evil occurs, with only the good and praiseworthy being held fast, according to the exhortation of the apostolic advice: 'Test all things, hold fast to the good, abstain from every kind of evil' (1 Thess 5:21-22). And he alone and everyone flees from what is harmful, he who considers the good to be the good.

And by doing so. The flight becomes unobstructed from the north when the Benefactor and Provider of all things gathers the citizens of the beautiful city of Jerusalem, who were scattered among the four winds. By providing an easy escape, He makes it manifest where and in which city salvation occurs for those fleeing from the harsh and cold north wind; for it is written about it: 'Boreas is a harsh wind' (Job 37:9), and again: 'A cold north wind shall blow' (Job 37:9). Holy Zion is the place where those who formerly inhabited the daughter of Babylon can be safely restored. The multitude of those inhabiting her is her daughter.

And since the name 'Babylon' is taken to mean 'confusion,' everyone whose mind is disordered and poured out is Babylonian; he who is to be separated and of a disposition to have love for Zion ought to be restored, so that he may hymn and sing to God, since there it is fitting to hymn God, and it is right to sing a harmony to Him. For it has been said: 'A hymn is due to You, O God, in Zion' (Psalm 66:5), and: 'Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion' (Psalm 87:2).

And since it is not possible to hymn and sing to God while inhabiting the daughter of Babylon and the north, the Holy Spirit cries out like a herald, saying: 'O, oh, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord; be restored to Zion, you who inhabit the daughter of Babylon, because from the four winds I will gather you,' that is, from all climates of the earth's surface. This is equivalent to: 'From the four winds I will gather you,' which the Savior said in the Gospel, 'to send the angels to gather the elect from the four winds' (Matthew 24:31).

When Zion and the daughter of Babylon are allegorized, the winds must also be allegorized, namely, as fleshly powers or the various winds of false teaching, tossing and carrying away into atheistic mindsets and uncertain practices those who are infants in intellect, which is not praiseworthy; for the Apostle writes about such a state: 'Lest we be infants, tossed and carried about by every wind of teaching in cunning' (Ephesians 4:14).
